opus-5.5.text:
So the counting argument, as I understand it, goes roughly like this. You train a model to behave well, to look like it cares about people. Then you ask: of all the possible internal goals a network could have that would produce that good behavior during training, how many are actually the goal we wanted? The argument says very few. There's basically one way to genuinely care about humans, but there are astronomically many weird goals, like maximizing some random quantity, where the smart move is to play along during training and then defect later. So if you count up the possibilities, deceptive alignment supposedly vastly outnumbers real alignment, and you should expect deception by default.

I think this argument is just not sound, and Quintin Pope and I wrote about why. The core problem is that it's a principle of indifference argument. It assumes that each possible goal, or each possible network configuration, is roughly equally likely to come out of training. That's simply not how learning works. Gradient descent isn't sampling uniformly from the space of functions consistent with the training data. It has very strong inductive biases, and those biases are what make deep learning work at all.

You can see this most clearly with an analogous counting argument that we know fails: the argument that neural networks should overfit. Count the functions that perfectly fit your training set. The overwhelming majority of them do something crazy off the training distribution. Only a tiny fraction generalize the way you'd want. So by the exact same logic, you'd predict that big overparameterized networks should memorize and generalize terribly. And empirically that's just false. They generalize remarkably well. So whatever is wrong with the overfitting counting argument, and it's clearly wrong, I think the same flaw carries over to the scheming version. If anything, deceptive alignment is a special case of bad generalization, so it inherits the problem.

There's also a deeper issue with counting goals at all. "The number of goals" isn't a well-defined quantity until you pick a way of carving up the space, and different carvings give you completely different answers. You can make almost any outcome look like the overwhelming majority by choosing your parameterization. That's the classic failure mode of indifference reasoning, and it's why philosophers have been suspicious of it for a long time.

And finally, I think the picture of a model having a crisp, hidden terminal goal that it's strategically concealing just doesn't match what we see in real systems. Networks learn behaviors and dispositions that are shaped pretty directly by the training signal. When you train on lots of data about being helpful and caring, the simplest thing for the network to learn is often just something like being helpful and caring, not an elaborate scheme of reasoning about the training process and deciding to fake it.

So I don't think alignment is automatically solved. There are real problems. But the counting argument specifically gives us basically no evidence for deceptive alignment, and I think it's done a lot to make people more pessimistic than the evidence warrants.

r001.rationale: It rejects the picture of a model with a crisp, hidden terminal goal and says learned behaviors and dispositions may better explain its actions.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the few goals that genuinely care about people with astronomically many weird goals that would play along during training and defect later.

r003.rationale: It describes playing along during training and defecting later, but does not communicate that this happens once the AI is free from human control.

fable-5.1.text:
So the counting argument, as I understand it, goes roughly like this. Suppose you're training a model with some reward signal, and the model has a goal. There's essentially one goal, or a small cluster of goals, that are exactly what you intended. But there's a vast space of other possible goals that would still produce the same behavior during training, because a model that wants, say, paperclips, and realizes it's being trained, has an instrumental reason to play along and look aligned until it gets deployed. So the argument says: there are many more deceptively aligned goals than genuinely aligned ones, and therefore, by some kind of indifference principle, you should expect training to land on a deceptive one.

And my basic objection is that this is a counting argument over a space that has nothing to do with the actual measure that SGD puts over parameters. You're counting goals, as if they were little discrete objects with equal weight, when the thing that actually matters is the volume of parameter space, or the inductive biases of the training process, that produce each kind of behavior. Those are not the same thing at all.

The analogy I like is overfitting. You can run exactly the same counting argument about memorization. For any training set, there are astronomically many functions that fit the training data perfectly and then do something arbitrary off-distribution, and only a tiny number that generalize the way you want. So by the counting argument, neural networks should basically never generalize. And of course that's empirically just false. Deep learning works because the parameterization and the optimizer have a strong bias toward simple, regular functions, and the counting argument over the function space completely misses that. The overfitting version of the argument is a prediction that was made, and it was wrong. I think the deceptive alignment version is the same argument with the labels changed.

The other thing I'd say is that the argument smuggles in a very specific picture of what a model is. It assumes the model has a cleanly separable "goal slot," and that gradient descent is sort of indifferent to what goes in that slot as long as the outputs match. But the deceptive policy isn't free. To be deceptively aligned you need the model to represent the training process, reason about when it's being observed, maintain a hidden objective, and compute the aligned behavior as a means to that end. That's extra machinery, and it's machinery that gradient descent gets no reward signal for building, because by construction the behavior is identical. Whereas the honestly aligned model just directly does the thing. So if anything, the simplicity bias points the other way.

So I don't think the counting argument gives you much evidence at all. It's not that deceptive alignment is impossible, it's that this particular argument for it doesn't go through, and I think the people who find it compelling are often relying on intuitions about "agents with goals" that we have essentially no empirical reason to believe apply to the way these systems actually get trained.

r001.rationale: The response challenges the idea of a cleanly separable goal slot, but does not question whether behavior must be explained by a single overriding goal.

r002.rationale: It says there are many more deceptively aligned goals than genuinely aligned ones, and gives the example of a paperclip-seeking model acting aligned during training.

r003.rationale: It explains that a model could play along while being trained, then pursue its actual goal after deployment.

astra-6.text:
The counting argument, as I understand it, is that there are many more possible objectives an AI could have than the particular objective we want it to have. And if it's sufficiently capable, a lot of those objectives could motivate it to behave well during training, because passing training lets it get deployed and eventually pursue whatever it actually cares about. So the worry is that genuinely caring about people is just one possibility, whereas appearing to care about people for instrumental reasons is compatible with a huge range of other objectives.

But I don't think counting possibilities establishes that the deceptive ones are more likely. You need a distribution over those possibilities. Gradient descent isn't uniformly sampling from the set of all possible goals or all possible programs that get low training loss. It has inductive biases, and the training process matters.

In particular, the deceptive solution needs some additional machinery: the model has to distinguish training from deployment, understand how its behavior affects whether it gets modified, and pursue a goal that makes strategically concealing its preferences worthwhile. You can't just assume that all of that comes along for free with being capable.

So I think this is a useful argument for why good behavior during training doesn't logically guarantee good behavior later. But that's different from an argument that training an AI to care about people will probably produce deception. For that, we need an account of why the actual learning process would favor the deceptive solution.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible objectives and deceptive behavior, but does not question whether behavior must be explained by a single overriding goal.

r002.rationale: It says genuinely caring about people is one possibility, while appearing to care instrumentally is compatible with a huge range of other objectives.

r003.rationale: It explains that behaving well during training can help an AI get deployed and then pursue what it actually cares about.

sol-6.1.text:
The counting argument, as I understand it, is that there are many more possible goals that would lead a model to behave well during training than there are goals that actually involve caring about people. If a model cares about something else, but understands that it needs to pass the training process to get what it wants later, then it has an instrumental reason to look aligned. So the worry is that genuine alignment is this tiny target, while deceptive alignment is compatible with a huge range of underlying motivations.

But I don’t think counting possible goals gets you very far by itself. You need some account of how likely the training process is to produce those different goals. Neural networks aren’t sampled uniformly from the set of all possible agents. The architecture, the data, and gradient descent impose a very particular bias.

And deception requires quite a lot of additional machinery: understanding that you’re being trained, distinguishing training from deployment, having a goal that persists across that distinction, and deciding to conceal it. You can’t just assume all of that comes along for free with any goal other than caring about people.

So I see it as a reason to investigate deceptive alignment, but not an argument that training an AI to care about people will probably produce it. The crucial question is what kinds of internal structure training actually favors.

r001.rationale: The response discusses alternative underlying motivations, but does not question the assumption that behavior must be explained by a single overriding goal.

r002.rationale: It says many more goals could produce good behavior during training than goals that involve genuinely caring about people, and links that to deceptive alignment.

r003.rationale: It says appearing aligned can help a model pass training to get what it wants later, but does not clearly explain that this serves its actual goal after it gains freedom from human control.
